## 4. Monotonicity formula and consequences

Let $(\widetilde{M},g)$ and $\Omega,U\subset\widetilde{M}$ be as given in Section 3.1. Throughout this section, we assume $u\in C^{\infty}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ is a solution to

$$ -\varepsilon\Delta u+\frac{W^{\prime}(u)}{\varepsilon}=\lambda\quad\text{in $\Omega\cap U$,} $$

$$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\text{on $\partial\Omega\cap U$}, $$

where $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ , $|\lambda|\leq\Lambda_{0}$ , $\|u\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{0}$ and $E_{\varepsilon}(u)\leq E_{0}$ . We define the energy density $e_{\epsilon}(u)$ and discrepancy function $\xi_{\varepsilon}(u)$ respectively by

$$ e_{\varepsilon}(u):=\frac{\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon} $$

and

$$ \xi_{\varepsilon}(u):=\frac{\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}-\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}. $$

Our first goal is to prove an almost-monotonicity inequality (c.f. [17, Appendix B]) of the form:

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(e^{c\rho}\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{B_{\rho}(x)\cap\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}(u)\right)\geq e^{c\rho}\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{B_{\rho}(x)\cap\Omega}-(\xi_{\varepsilon}(u))^{+} $$

for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently small $\rho$ . Next, we establish up-to-the-boundary estimates, in both pointwise and integral forms, for $u$ and $\xi_{\varepsilon}(u)$ . Together with the almost-monotonicity inequality, these estimates allow us to control the energy density ratio

$$ I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x):=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}(u) $$

which will be instrumental in deriving the regularity of the limit interface in later sections.

### 4.1. Almost monotonicity formula

Recall that the monotonicity formula for minimal surfaces is obtained by applying the first variation formula for the area functional with (suitably truncated) radial test vector fields. In the Allen-Cahn setting, the almost monotonicity formula (which can be viewed as an $\varepsilon$ -version of the monotonicity formula for minimal surfaces) can be obtained by similar arguments. The following Pohozaev identity plays the role of the first variation formula in this regard.

#### Lemma 4.1 (Pohozaev identity).

Let $u\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ be a solution to the semilinear equation $\Delta u=F(u)$ in $\Omega\cap U$ where $F=G^{\prime}$ for some smooth function $G:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ . For any $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Omega\cap U}\left[\left(\frac{|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+G(u)\right)\operatorname{div}_{g}X-\nabla X(\nabla u,\nabla u)\right]\;dv_{g} \displaystyle=\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\left[\left(\frac{|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+G(u)\right)(X\cdot\nu)-(\nabla u\cdot X)\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}\right] \displaystyle d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

#### Proof.

Multiply both sides of the equation $\Delta u=F(u)$ by $X\cdot\nabla u$ and then integrate by part twice (see [43, Lemma 9] for a similar calculation). ∎

For the Allen-Cahn equation (4.1), we choose $G(t)=\varepsilon^{-2}\widetilde{W}(t)$ where

$$ \widetilde{W}(t):=W(t)-\varepsilon\lambda t+\varepsilon\Lambda_{0}C_{0}. $$

Note that the constant term $\varepsilon\Lambda_{0}C_{0}$ is there simply to ensure that $\widetilde{W}(u)\geq 0$ under our assumptions. For this choice of $G$ and using the Neumann boundary condition (4.2), the Pohozaev identity (4.6) reads

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Omega\cap U}\left[\left(\frac{\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{\widetilde{W}(u)}{\varepsilon}\right)\operatorname{div}_{g}X-\varepsilon\nabla X(\nabla u,\nabla u)\right]\;dv_{g} \displaystyle=\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\left(\frac{\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{\widetilde{W}(u)}{\varepsilon}\right)(X\cdot\nu)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1} \displaystyle. $$

We define $\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)$ , $\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}(u)$ and $\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)$ as in (4.3), (4.4) and (4.5) similarly with $W$ replaced by $\widetilde{W}$ . We will first establish the almost monotonicity formula for $\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}$ from which the corresponding almost monotonicity formula for $I_{\varepsilon,u}$ follows.

For the purpose of making the test vector fields compactly supported, we let $\varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be any smooth decreasing cutoff function such that $\varphi(t)=1$ for $t\leq\frac{1}{2}$ and $\varphi(t)=0$ for $t\geq 1$ . For any $x\in\widetilde{M}$ and $0<\rho<\operatorname{inj}_{g}(x)$ , the function $\varphi\left(\frac{\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\cdot)}{\rho}\right)$ is a smooth function which is compactly supported inside $B_{\rho}(x)$ .

From now on, we fix $x\in U\cap\overline{\Omega}$ and denote $r(\cdot):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\cdot)$ . For any $0<\rho<\min\{\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U),i_{0}\}$ , we consider the test vector field $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ defined by

$$ X:=\varphi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)r\nabla r $$

which is a truncated radial vector field centered at $x$ supported inside $B_{\rho}(x)$ . When $\rho<\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}}$ , a direct computation together with (2.1) and (2.2) gives

$$ \left|\operatorname{div}_{g}X(x)-\left(n\varphi+\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}\right)\right|\leq(n-1)\sqrt{k_{0}}r\varphi $$

and

$$ \left|\nabla X(\nabla u,\nabla u)-\left(|\nabla u|^{2}\varphi+\frac{r}{\rho}(\nabla u\cdot\nabla r)^{2}\varphi^{\prime}\right)\right|\leq\sqrt{k_{0}}r|\nabla u|^{2}\varphi $$

where $\varphi$ and $\varphi^{\prime}$ are both evaluated at $\frac{r}{\rho}$ by abuse of notation. Observing the relation

$$ \rho\frac{d}{d\rho}\left[\varphi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\right]=-\frac{r}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right). $$

and plugging the above estimates into the left hand side of the Pohozaev identity (4.7), we obtain the inequality

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{d\rho} \displaystyle\left[\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\Omega\cap U}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\varphi\right]-\rho^{-(n-1)}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left[\int_{\Omega\cap U}\varepsilon(\nabla u\cdot\nabla r)^{2}\varphi\right]+\rho^{-n}\int_{\Omega\cap U}\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}(u)\varphi \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle-(n+1)\sqrt{k_{0}}\left[\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\Omega\cap U}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\varphi\right]-\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\partial\Omega\cap U}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)|\nabla r\cdot\nu|\varphi\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

Note that we have used the fact that $r\leq\rho$ in the support of $\varphi$ and $\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}\leq 2\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)$ . We would like to consider two separate cases:

- • Case 1: $x\in\Omega\cap U$ and $B_{\rho}(x)\Subset\Omega\cap U$ ;

- • Case 2: $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ $B_{\rho}(x)\Subset U$ .

In the first case, there is no boundary term as $B_{\rho}(x)\cap\partial\Omega=\emptyset$ . We obtain the following interior almost-monotonicity inequality (c.f. [17, Appendix B]), which reduces to [21, Lemma 3.1] when $k_{0}=0$ .

#### Lemma 4.2 (Interior almost-monotonicity inequality).

For any $x\in\Omega\cap U$ and $0<\rho<\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}}\}$ such that $B_{\rho}(x)\Subset\Omega\cap U$ , we have

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left[e^{(n+1)\sqrt{k_{0}}\rho}\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\right]\geq e^{(n+1)\sqrt{k_{0}}\rho}\rho^{-n}\int_{B_{\rho}(x)}-\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}(u). $$

#### Proof.

It follows directly from (4.8) by dropping the non-negative term and the boundary term. Finally, we let $\varphi\to\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,1)}$ . ∎

For the second case, we need to handle the extra boundary term in (4.8). The following lemma allows us to rewrite the boundary term in terms of an interior integral (and its derivative).

#### Lemma 4.3.

For any $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $0<\rho<\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\}$ such that $B_{\rho}(x)\Subset U$ , we have

$$ \int_{\partial\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\leq(n+1)C_{2}\int_{\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)+6\frac{d}{d\rho}\left[\int_{\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\right]. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\varphi$ be the radial cutoff function centered at $x$ as defined before. For any $0<\rho<\min\{\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U),\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\}$ , we can consider the test vector field $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ defined by

$$ X=-\varphi\left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)\nabla d $$

where $d$ is the signed distance function from $\partial\Omega$ as defined in section 2.2. Note that $X$ is smooth and compactly supported in $B_{\rho}(x)$ with $X\cdot\nu=\varphi$ along $\partial\Omega$ . By (2.6), we have the following estimates:

$$ \operatorname{div}_{g}X\leq(n-1)C_{1}\varphi-\frac{1}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime} $$

$$ -\varepsilon\nabla X(\nabla u,\nabla u)\leq\left(C_{1}\varphi-\frac{1}{\rho}\varphi^{\prime}\right)\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}. $$

Putting all these into the Pohozaev identity (4.7), noting that $r\geq\frac{\rho}{2}$ in the support of $\varphi^{\prime}$ and $\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}\leq 2\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)$ , and then letting $\varphi\to\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,1)}$ , we obtain the desired inequality. ∎

We are now ready to establish the almost-monotonicity inequality centered at a boundary point $x\in\partial\Omega$ .

#### Lemma 4.4 (Boundary almost-monotonicity inequality).

There exists a constant

$$ c_{1}=c_{1}(n,k_{0},\kappa_{0})\geq 0 $$

so that the following holds: for any $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ and $0<\rho<\frac{1}{2}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}}\}$ such that $B_{\rho}(x)\Subset U$ , we have

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left[e^{c_{1}\rho}\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\right]\geq\frac{e^{c_{1}\rho}}{1+3\kappa_{0}\rho}\rho^{-n}\int_{\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}-\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}(u). $$

#### Proof.

First of all, note that by (2.7), we have the following estimate on the boundary term of (4.8) for any $\rho<\frac{1}{2}i_{0}$ ,

$$ \rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\partial\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)|\nabla r\cdot\nu|\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\leq\frac{\kappa_{0}}{2}\rho^{-(n-2)}\int_{\partial\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

On the other hand, Lemma 4.3 implies that when $\rho<\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{2\kappa_{0}}\}$ , we have the inequality

$$ \displaystyle 6\rho\frac{d}{d\rho}\left[\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\right]\geq \displaystyle\rho^{-(n-2)}\int_{\partial\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u)\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1} \displaystyle-[(n+1)C_{1}\rho+6(n-1)]\rho^{-(n-1)}\int_{\Omega\cap B_{\rho}(x)}\widetilde{e}_{\varepsilon}(u). $$

Putting it back to (4.8), using $\rho\kappa_{0}<\frac{1}{2}$ , after letting $\varphi\to\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,1)}$ and rearranging terms gives the desired inequality with $c_{1}=\frac{n+1}{4}C_{1}+3(n-1)\kappa_{0}$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.5.

As noted in the Introduction, it would be possible to mimic the approach of [15] and [39], by reflecting across the boundary $\partial\Omega$ , and prove an almost-monotonicity inequality for the sum of the energy density ratio on a ball centered in $\overline{\Omega}$ and its reflection. We chose, for the sake of simplicity, to avoid reflection across the boundary entirely, and consider balls that are either disjoint from $\partial\Omega$ , or centered at points lying on $\partial\Omega$ , as in [16].

### 4.2. Auxiliary estimates

We first derive some a-priori estimates for any solution $u$ to (4.1) and (4.2). These estimates hold locally uniformly in space up to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ and uniformly in $\varepsilon$ . We fix throughout this subsection an open subset $\tilde{U}\Subset U$ .

We begin with the $C^{0}$ -estimate. Our proof uses a maximum principle argument similar to that in [21, Proposition 3.2], except that we have to include an extra barrier term to prevent the extrema from occurring along the boundary.

#### Lemma 4.6 (Uniform $C^{0}$ estimate).

There exist constants

$$ \varepsilon_{2}=\varepsilon_{2}(\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{2}=c_{2}(\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))\geq 1 $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{2}$ , we have

$$ \|u\|_{C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U})}\leq 1+c_{2}\varepsilon<2 $$

#### Proof.

Let $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}$ and $\rho<\frac{1}{6}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)\}$ . Denote $r(\cdot):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\cdot)$ . Inside the ball $B_{3\rho}(x)\Subset U$ , we fix a smooth radial function $\zeta=\zeta(r)$ such that

- • $\zeta=1+\frac{c_{2}\varepsilon}{2}$ inside $B_{\rho}(x)$ ;

- • $\zeta=1+C_{0}$ on the annulus $B_{3\rho}(x)\setminus B_{2\rho}(x)$ ; and

- • inside the ball $B_{3\rho}(x)$ , we have by (2.2)

$$ 1+\frac{c_{2}\varepsilon}{2}\leq\zeta\leq 1+C_{0},\quad|\nabla\zeta|\leq 2C_{0}\rho^{-1},\quad|\Delta\zeta|\leq C(n)C_{0}\rho^{-2} $$

where $c_{2}$ will be chosen later and then $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small so that $c_{2}\varepsilon<\min\{1,C_{0}\}$ .

We first claim that $u\leq 1+c_{2}\varepsilon$ on $B_{\rho}(x)\cap\Omega$ for all sufficiently small $\rho$ by a contradiction argument. Suppose we have $\sup_{B_{\rho}(x)\cap\Omega}u>1+c_{2}\varepsilon$ . We divide into two cases as before:

- • Case 1: $x\in\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ and $B_{3\rho}(x)\Subset\Omega\cap U$ ;

- • Case 2: $x\in\partial\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ and $B_{3\rho}(x)\Subset U$ .

For the first case, we consider as in [21, Proposition 3.2] the auxiliary function $f:=u-\zeta$ which is smooth inside $B_{3\rho}(x)$ . One can verify

- • $f\leq-1$ along the boundary $\partial B_{3\rho}(x)$ , and

- • $\sup_{B_{3\rho}(x)}f>\frac{c_{2}\varepsilon}{2}>0$ .

Therefore, $f(x_{0})=\sup_{B_{3\rho}(x)}f>\frac{c_{2}\varepsilon}{2}$ at an interior maxima $x_{0}\in B_{3\rho}(x)$ . By maximum principle, at $x_{0}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle 0\geq\varepsilon\Delta f= \displaystyle\varepsilon^{-1}W^{\prime}(u)-\lambda-\varepsilon\Delta\zeta \displaystyle= \displaystyle\varepsilon^{-1}\left.W^{\prime}(tu+(1-t)\zeta)\right|_{t=0}^{t=1}+\varepsilon^{-1}W^{\prime}(\zeta)-\lambda-\varepsilon\Delta\zeta \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\varepsilon^{-1}f\int_{0}^{1}W^{\prime\prime}(tu+(1-t)\zeta)\;dt-\lambda-\varepsilon\Delta\zeta \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\frac{c_{2}\kappa}{2}-\lambda-\varepsilon\Delta\zeta, $$

Note that we have used that $u>\zeta\geq 1$ at $x_{0}$ and the properties of $W$ in section 2.5. If $c_{2}\geq 1$ is sufficiently large, depending only on $\Lambda_{0}$ , $C_{0}$ , $W$ , $n$ , $i_{0}$ , $k_{0}$ , $\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U)$ and $\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega)$ , we arrive at a contradiction.

For the second case, we consider another auxiliary function

$$ f:=u-\zeta+\frac{4C_{0}}{\rho}\chi_{a}\circ d $$

where $d(\cdot)=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$ and $\chi$ is the cutoff function defined in section 2.6 with $a=\frac{\varepsilon\rho}{16C_{0}}$ . One can again verify

- • $f\leq-1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}<-\frac{1}{2}$ along the boundary $\partial B_{3\rho}(x)\cap\Omega$ ;

- • $\sup_{B_{3\rho}(x)\cap\Omega}f>\frac{c_{2}\varepsilon}{2}>0$ ; and

- • $\frac{\partial f}{\partial\nu}\leq-2C_{0}\rho^{-1}<0$ along $B_{3\rho}(x)\cap\partial\Omega$ .

Hence, $\sup_{B_{3\rho}(x)\cap\Omega}f$ is again achieved by an interior maxima $x_{0}\in B_{3\rho}(x)\cap\Omega$ . Applying the maximum principle at $x_{0}$ , a similar calculation as before (note that we still have $u\geq 1$ and $\zeta>1$ by our choice of $a$ ) gives

$$ \frac{c_{2}\kappa}{2}\leq\lambda+\varepsilon\Delta\zeta+\frac{1}{2}\max_{t\in[1,1+C_{0}]}W^{\prime\prime}(t)-\frac{4\varepsilon C_{0}}{\rho}\Delta(\chi_{a}\circ d). $$

By the definition of $\chi_{a}$ in section 2.6 and (2.6), we will again obtain a contradiction when $c_{2}$ is sufficiently large, depending only on $\Lambda_{0}$ , $C_{0}$ , $W$ , $n$ , $i_{0}$ , $k_{0}$ , $\kappa_{0}$ and $\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U)$ . This proves the desired upper bound for $u$ . The lower bound can be obtained similarly by considering the auxiliary function $f=u+\zeta$ for Case 1 and $f=u+\zeta-\frac{4C_{0}}{\rho}\chi_{a}\circ d$ for Case 2. ∎

Using the $C^{0}$ -estimate in Lemma 4.6, one obtains up-to-the-boundary gradient estimates by standard PDE theory of semi-linear elliptic equations.

#### Lemma 4.7 (Uniform gradient estimates).

There exists a constant

$$ c_{3}=c_{3}(\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))\geq 1 $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{2}$ , we have the gradient estimate

$$ \|\varepsilon\nabla u\|_{C^{0}(\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U})}\leq c_{3}. $$

#### Proof.

The interior gradient estimate can be found e.g. in [19, Proposition 2.19]. The boundary gradient estimates along $\partial\Omega$ follows e.g. from [44, Theorem 1.1] (c.f. [45] for the extension to the Riemannian setting). ∎

We can actually obtain better estimates away from the transition region $\{|u|\leq\alpha\}$ which imply that $\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}$ is of order $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2\eta-1})$ for any $\eta\in(0,1)$ .

#### Lemma 4.8 (Refined uniform $C^{0}$ estimates away from the transition region).

For any $\eta\in(0,1)$ , there exist constants

$$ \varepsilon_{4}=\varepsilon_{4}(\eta,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{4}=c_{4}(\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))\geq 1 $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{4}$ , $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}$ and $\varepsilon^{1-\eta}\leq r\leq\frac{1}{6}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)\}$ , we have

- (i) if $u\geq\alpha$ on $B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega$ , then $1-c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}\leq u\leq 1+c_{4}\varepsilon$ on $B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega$ ;

- (ii) if $u\leq-\alpha$ on $B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega$ , then $-1-c_{4}\varepsilon\leq u\leq-1+c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}$ on $B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega$ .

#### Proof.

We only prove (i) as the arguments are the same for (ii). Let $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}$ and $r<\frac{1}{6}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)\}$ . Suppose $u\geq\alpha$ on $B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega$ . By Lemma 4.6, we have $u\leq 1+c_{2}\varepsilon$ provided that $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{2}$ . It remains to prove that $u\geq 1-c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}$ on $B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega$ for some suitable choice of $c_{4}$ , range of $r$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ .

We will argue by contradiction as in the proof of Lemma 4.6. Suppose, on the contrary, that $\alpha\leq\inf_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}u<1-c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}$ . We fix a smooth radial function $\zeta$ such that

- • $\zeta=1-\frac{c_{4}\kappa\varepsilon^{\eta}}{4C}$ inside $B_{r}(x)$ ;

- • $\zeta=\alpha+\frac{c_{4}\kappa\varepsilon^{\eta}}{4C}$ on the annulus $B_{3r}(x)\setminus B_{2r}(x)$ ; and

- • inside the ball $B_{3r}(x)$ , we have by (2.2)

$$ \alpha+\frac{c_{4}\kappa\varepsilon^{\eta}}{4C}\leq\zeta\leq 1-\frac{c_{4}\kappa\varepsilon^{\eta}}{4C},\quad|\nabla\zeta|\leq 2r^{-1},\quad|\Delta\zeta|\leq C(n)r^{-2} $$

where $C=C(W):=\max\{1,\max_{s\in[\alpha,2]}|W^{\prime\prime}(s)|\}$ , $c_{4}$ will be chosen later and then $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small so that $c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}<\min\{1,\frac{2C(1-\alpha)}{\kappa}\}$ .

We now consider the auxiliary function

$$ f:=u-\zeta+\frac{4}{r}\chi_{a}\circ d $$

where $d(\cdot)=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$ and $\chi$ is the cutoff function defined in section 2.6 with $a=\frac{c_{4}\kappa r\varepsilon^{\eta}}{16C}$ . One can verify (note that $C\geq\kappa$ )

- • $f\geq-\frac{3}{4}\frac{c_{4}\kappa\varepsilon^{\eta}}{C}\geq-\frac{3}{4}c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}$ along the boundary $\partial B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega$ ;

- • $\inf_{B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega}f<-\frac{3}{4}c_{4}\varepsilon^{\eta}$ ; and

- • $\frac{\partial f}{\partial\nu}\geq\frac{2}{r}>0$ along $B_{3r}(x)\cap\partial\Omega$ , if non-empty.

Hence, no matter whether $x\in\Omega$ or $x\in\partial\Omega$ , $\inf_{B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega}f$ is achieved by an interior minima $x_{0}\in B_{3r}(x)\cap\Omega$ . Applying the maximum principle at $x_{0}$ , by our choice of $a$ and a similar calculation as before (note that we still have $\alpha\leq u(x_{0})<2$ and $\alpha\leq\zeta(x_{0})\leq 1$ ) gives

$$ \frac{3c_{4}\kappa}{4}\varepsilon^{-1+\eta}\leq-\lambda-\varepsilon\Delta\zeta-\frac{4\varepsilon}{r}\Delta(\chi_{a}\circ d). $$

By the definition of $\chi_{a}$ in section 2.6 and (2.6), this implies

$$ \frac{3\kappa}{4}c_{4}\leq\Lambda_{0}\varepsilon^{1-\eta}+C(n)\varepsilon^{2-\eta}r^{-2}+4(n-1)C_{2}\varepsilon^{2-\eta}r^{-1}+\frac{32C}{c_{4}\kappa}\varepsilon^{2-2\eta}r^{-2}. $$

For $r\geq\varepsilon^{1-\eta}$ , this yields a contradiction when $c_{4}$ is sufficiently large, depending only on $\Lambda_{0}$ , $W$ , $n$ , $i_{0}$ , $k_{0}$ , $\kappa_{0}$ and $\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U)$ . ∎

#### Remark 4.9.

In case $B_{3r}(x)\Subset\Omega$ , we do not need to include the term involving $\chi_{a}$ in the auxiliary function $f$ and we have the stronger conclusion that $u\geq 1-c_{4}\varepsilon$ (i.e. with $\eta=1$ ), c.f. [21, Proposition 4.1]. With a different choice of auxiliary function $\zeta$ , we can also establish the same estimates with $\eta=1$ . However, unlike in [21] (see the remark after Proposition 3.2), apparently one cannot obtain better estimates even when $\lambda=0$ by iterating the arguments above.

### 4.3. Estimates for the discrepancy function

Note that in order for the almost-monotonicity formula in Lemma 4.2 and 4.4 to be effective, we need some control on the right hand side of the inequalities involving the discrepancy function $\xi_{\varepsilon}$ defined in (4.4).

We give in this subsection a crude pointwise upper bound for the discrepancy function. We want to point out that our bound is weaker than the interior bound obtained in [21, Proposition 3.3] but holds up to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ . Note that we have chosen to work at the original scale, rather than rescaling by $\varepsilon$ as in [21]. This does not affect our subsequent analysis, but certain expressions will change by appropriate multiples of $\varepsilon$ .

#### Proposition 4.10 (Pointwise upper bound on discrepancy function).

There exists a constant

$$ \varepsilon_{5}=\varepsilon_{5}(\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{5}$ , we have

$$ \sup_{\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}}\xi_{\varepsilon}(u)\leq\varepsilon^{-4/5}. $$

#### Proof.

We consider as in [21] the following auxiliary function

$$ \xi_{G}:=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}-\varepsilon^{-1}W(u)-\varepsilon^{-1}G(u) $$

where $G\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$ is to be chosen later. By Bochner’s formula (2.3) and a similar computation as in [21, Lemma 3.5], we have the following differential inequality at points where $|\nabla u|>0$ :

$$ \displaystyle\varepsilon^{2} \displaystyle\Delta\xi_{G}-\frac{2(W^{\prime}+G^{\prime})\nabla u}{|\nabla u|^{2}}\cdot\nabla\xi_{G}+2(G^{\prime\prime}+(n-1)k_{0}\varepsilon^{2})\xi_{G} \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\varepsilon^{-1}(G^{\prime})^{2}+\varepsilon^{-1}G^{\prime}W^{\prime}-2\varepsilon^{-1}(G^{\prime\prime}+(n-1)k_{0}\varepsilon^{2})(W+G)+\lambda(W^{\prime}+G^{\prime}) $$

where the functions $G$ and $W$ and their derivatives are evaluated at $u$ .

Let $\delta\in(0,1)$ to be fixed later and define (recall Lemma 4.6)

$$ G=G_{\delta}(r):=\delta\left(1+\int_{-1-c_{2}\varepsilon_{2}}^{r}\exp\left(-\int_{-1-c_{2}\varepsilon_{2}}^{t}\frac{|W^{\prime}(s)|+\delta}{2(W(s)+\delta)}\;ds\right)\;dt\right). $$

Noting that $\frac{W}{W^{\prime}}$ is a smooth function which vanishes at $\pm 1$ , one easily verifies that the following holds on $r\in[-1-c_{2}\varepsilon_{2},1+c_{2}\varepsilon_{2}]$ ,

- • $\delta\leq G\leq 5\delta$ ,

- • $C^{-1}\delta^{2}<G^{\prime}\leq\delta$ ,

- • $0<-G^{\prime\prime}=G^{\prime}\frac{|W^{\prime}(r)|+\delta}{2(W(r)+\delta)}\leq C$

for some constant $C=C(W)>1$ . By Lemma 4.6, we have (the functions $G$ and $W$ and their derivatives are evaluated at $u$ )

$$ G^{\prime}W^{\prime}-2G^{\prime\prime}(W+G)=G^{\prime}\left(W^{\prime}+\frac{|W^{\prime}|+\delta}{W+\delta}(W+G)\right)\geq\delta G^{\prime} $$

provided that $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{2}$ .

Let $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}$ and $R=\frac{1}{6}\min\{i_{0},\frac{1}{\sqrt{k_{0}}},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U),1\}$ . We fix a smooth radial cutoff function $\zeta$ centered at $x$ such that

- • $\zeta=1$ on $B_{R/8}(x)$

- • $\zeta=0$ outside $B_{R/4}(x)$ ,

- • $0\leq\zeta\leq 1$ , $|\nabla\zeta|\leq 8R^{-1}\zeta^{1/2}$ , $|\Delta\zeta|\leq C(n)R^{-2}$

where $C(n)>0$ is a constant depending only on $n$ . Let $d(\cdot):=\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\cdot,\partial\Omega)$ and $\chi$ be the cutoff function defined in section 2.6 with $a=(8\hat{C})^{-1}\varepsilon^{1/5}R$ where $\hat{C}>0$ is a constant to be fixed later. Define a new auxiliary function

$$ f:=\zeta\xi_{G}+\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\chi_{a}\circ d. $$

We claim that for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ , we have

$$ \sup_{\Omega}f\leq\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{-4/5}. $$

If the supremum is non-positive, then we must have $\xi_{G}\leq 0$ and by our choice of $G$ that

$$ \xi_{\varepsilon}=\xi_{G}+\varepsilon^{-1}G(u)\leq 5\varepsilon^{-1}\delta $$

and thus $\xi_{\varepsilon}(x)\leq\varepsilon^{-4/5}$ provided that $\delta\leq\frac{1}{5}\varepsilon^{1/5}$ . So, without loss of generality, we assume that $\sup_{\Omega}f>0$ and is achieved at some point $x_{0}\in B_{R/4}(x)\cap\overline{\Omega}$ (note that $f\leq\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon^{-4/5}$ outside $B_{R/4}(x)$ by our choice of $a$ ). First, we claim that $x_{0}\notin\partial\Omega$ . By the Neumann boundary condition (4.2) and [39, Lemma 3.1], along $\partial\Omega$ we have

$$ \frac{\partial f}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial\zeta}{\partial\nu}\xi_{G}-\varepsilon\zeta B(\nabla u,\nabla u)-\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C} $$

where $B$ is the second fundamental form of $\partial\Omega$ with respect to $\nu$ (i.e. $B(\tau,\tau):=\langle\nabla_{\tau}\nu,\tau\rangle$ ). Since $\kappa_{0}$ bounds the maximum absolute value of the principal curvatures of $\partial\Omega$ , by Lemma 4.7 and our choice of $\zeta$ , we have $\frac{\partial f}{\partial\nu}<0$ along $\partial\Omega$ by taking $\hat{C}:=10c_{3}^{2}$ . Hence, we can assume without loss of generality that $x_{0}\notin\partial\Omega$ . Suppose (4.19) does not hold, then at an interior maximum $x_{0}$ we have by our choice of $a$ that

$$ \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon\zeta|\nabla u|^{2}\geq\zeta\xi_{G}>\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{-4/5}-2a\hat{C}\epsilon^{-1}R^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon^{-4/5}. $$

From this and (4.14), we have at $x_{0}$ ,

$$ \xi_{G}\leq\frac{c_{3}^{2}}{2}\varepsilon^{-1}\quad\text{ and }\quad\zeta^{-1}\leq 2c_{3}^{2}\varepsilon^{-1/5}. $$

Since $x_{0}$ is an interior maximum point of $f$ , we have $\nabla f=0$ and $\Delta f\leq 0$ at $x_{0}$ . The first order condition says $\zeta\nabla\xi_{G}=-\xi_{G}\nabla\zeta-\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\chi_{a}^{\prime}\nabla d$ , which together with (4.22) implies

$$ \zeta^{1/2}|\nabla\xi_{G}|\leq 4c_{3}^{2}\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}+\sqrt{2}\hat{C}c_{3}\varepsilon^{-11/10}R^{-1}\leq C(c_{3})\varepsilon^{-11/10}R^{-1}. $$

On the other hand, the second order condition at $x_{0}$ says

$$ \zeta\Delta\xi_{G}\leq-\xi_{G}\Delta\zeta-2\nabla\zeta\cdot\nabla\xi_{G}-\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\chi_{a}^{\prime}\Delta d-\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\chi_{a}^{\prime\prime}|\nabla d|^{2}. $$

Using the first order condition, our choice of $\zeta$ , together with (2.6) and (4.22), we have

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\xi_{G} \displaystyle\leq\Big(-\xi_{G}\zeta^{-1}\Delta\zeta+2\xi_{G}\zeta^{-2}|\nabla\zeta|^{2}\Big)+2\zeta^{-2}\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\chi_{a}^{\prime}(\nabla d\cdot\nabla\zeta) \displaystyle-\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\zeta^{-1}\chi_{a}^{\prime}\Delta d-\varepsilon^{-1}R^{-1}\hat{C}\zeta^{-1}\chi_{a}^{\prime\prime}|\nabla d|^{2} \displaystyle\leq C(n,c_{3})\varepsilon^{-6/5}R^{-2}+C(c_{3})\varepsilon^{-13/10}R^{-2} \displaystyle+C(C_{1},c_{3},n)\varepsilon^{-6/5}R^{-1}+C(c_{3})\varepsilon^{-7/5}R^{-2} \displaystyle\leq C(C_{1},c_{3},n)\varepsilon^{-7/5}R^{-2}. $$

Combining the estimates above, for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ depending only on $C_{1}$ , $n$ , $\hat{C}$ and $c_{3}$ , we have at $x_{0}$

$$ \textrm{(L.H.S.) of \eqref{E:xi-inequality}}\leq C(C_{1},c_{3},n)\varepsilon^{3/5}R^{-2}+C(W,c_{3})\varepsilon^{-1/5}R^{-1}+C(n,k_{0},c_{3})\varepsilon $$

On the other hand, by our choice of $G$ , together with (4.18)

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{(R.H.S.) of \eqref{E:xi-inequality}} \displaystyle\geq\varepsilon^{-1}(G^{\prime})^{2}+\varepsilon^{-1}\delta G^{\prime}-C(n,k_{0},W)\varepsilon-C(W)\Lambda_{0} \displaystyle\geq\varepsilon^{-1}(C^{-2}\delta^{4}+C^{-1}\delta^{3})-C(n,k_{0},W)\varepsilon-C(W)\Lambda_{0} \displaystyle\geq 2C^{-2}\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{4}-C(n,k_{0},W)\varepsilon-C(W)\Lambda_{0}. $$

Combining these we arrive at the inequality

$$ \delta^{4}\leq C^{\prime\prime}\varepsilon^{4/5} $$

for some constant $C^{\prime\prime}>0$ depending only on $\Lambda_{0}$ , $C_{0}$ , $W$ , $n$ , $i_{0}$ , $k_{0}$ , $\kappa_{0}$ and $\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U)$ . Therefore, we arrive at a contradiction by taking $\delta=(2C^{\prime\prime})^{1/4}\varepsilon^{1/5}<1$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ . Therefore, (4.19) holds and Proposition 4.10 follows. ∎

#### Remark 4.11.

With a different choice of the auxiliary function $G$ , resembling the one in [22], it is possible to obtain a better estimate of order $\varepsilon^{-3/5}$ in Proposition 4.10.

### 4.4. Consequences of the almost monotonicity formula

We now combine the results obtained in the previous subsections to derive some consequences of the almost monotonicity formula (Lemma 4.2 and 4.4). We first establish a uniform lower bound of the energy density ratio (4.5) on balls of radius $\varepsilon\leq r\leq\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{4/5})$ centered at a boundary point within the transition region $\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ .

#### Lemma 4.12 (Energy density ratio lower bound I).

For any $b\in(0,1-\alpha)$ , there exist constants

$$ \varepsilon_{6}=\varepsilon_{6}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{6}=c_{6}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0 $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{4}$ , $x\in\partial\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ with $|u(x)|\leq 1-b$ , and $\varepsilon\leq r\leq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ , we have

$$ I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\geq c_{6}. $$

In fact, the same holds for $x\in\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ provided furthermore that $r<\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega)$ .

#### Proof.

We first assume $x\in\partial\Omega$ . Since $|u(x)|\leq 1-b$ , we have $|u|\leq 1-\frac{b}{2}$ on $B_{\frac{b\varepsilon}{2c_{3}}}(x)\cap\Omega$ by (4.14) provided that $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{2}$ . As a result, by (2.8) and (4.5) we have for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ that

$$ \widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\varepsilon,x)\geq I_{\varepsilon,u}(\varepsilon,x)\geq\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}\varepsilon^{n-1}}\int_{B_{\frac{b\varepsilon}{2c_{3}}}(p)\cap\Omega}\frac{W(u)}{\varepsilon}\geq 4c^{\prime}_{6} $$

where $c^{\prime}_{6}:=\frac{1}{12}\frac{\omega_{n}}{\omega_{n-1}}\left(\frac{b}{2c_{3}}\right)^{n}\min_{|s|\leq 1-\frac{b}{2}}W(s)>0$ .

Let $c_{6}^{\prime\prime}:=\frac{\omega_{n-1}}{\omega_{n}}c_{6}^{\prime}$ . Assuming $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{5}$ is sufficiently small such that $c_{6}^{\prime\prime}\varepsilon^{4/5}<\frac{1}{2}\min\{\operatorname{dist}(\tilde{U},\partial U),i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}}\}$ , we can apply the boundary almost monotonicity formula (4.11) and the upper bound on discrepancy function (4.15) to see that for any $\varepsilon\leq r\leq c_{6}^{\prime\prime}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ (note that $\widetilde{\xi}_{\varepsilon}(u)\leq\xi_{\varepsilon}(u)$ by definition)

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x) \displaystyle\geq e^{-c_{1}(r-\varepsilon)}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\varepsilon,x)-\frac{2}{3}\frac{\omega_{n}}{\omega_{n-1}}\varepsilon^{-4/5}(r-\varepsilon) \displaystyle\geq e^{-c_{1}c_{6}^{\prime}\varepsilon^{4/5}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\varepsilon,x)-\frac{2}{3}\frac{\omega_{n}}{\omega_{n-1}}c_{6}^{\prime\prime}>2c_{6}^{\prime} $$

for $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small such that (4.25) holds and $e^{-c_{1}c_{6}^{\prime}\varepsilon^{4/5}}\geq\frac{3}{4}$ . Setting $c_{6}:=\min\{c_{6}^{\prime},c_{6}^{\prime\prime}\}$ , the asserted lower bound for $I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)$ follows from the estimate

$$ \widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)+\frac{4}{3}\frac{\omega_{n}}{\omega_{n-1}}\Lambda_{0}C_{0}r $$

which holds for all sufficiently small $r$ depending only on $k_{0}$ and $\kappa_{0}$ . The case for interior points $x\in\Omega$ can be obtained similarly using the interior monotonicity formula (4.9). ∎

In order to prove a uniform lower bound of the energy density ratio on balls of radius $r\geq\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{4/5})$ , the pointwise upper bound in Proposition 4.10 will not be sufficient for our purpose. We need a more refined integral upper bound for the discrepancy function. It is important to note that the center $x$ in the proposition below may or may not lie in $\partial\Omega$ , and does not need to be inside the transition region $\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ .

#### Proposition 4.13 (Integral upper bound for discrepancy function).

For any $b\in(0,1-\alpha)$ , there exist constants

$$ r_{2}=r_{2}(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))\in(0,1), $$

$$ \varepsilon_{7}=\varepsilon_{7}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{7}=c_{7}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>1 $$

such that for any $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{7}$ , $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}$ and $c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}\leq r\leq r_{2}$ , we have

$$ \frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\xi_{\varepsilon}^{+}(u)\leq\frac{c_{7}}{r^{7/8}}(I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)+1). $$

#### Proof.

Let $b\in(0,1-\alpha)$ . Fix $x\in\overline{\Omega}\cap\tilde{U}$ and $c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}\leq r\leq r_{2}$ where $r_{2}$ is sufficiently small with $r_{2}<\frac{1}{2}\{r_{0},r_{1},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial U)\}$ . We divide the domain of integration $B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega$ into a union of three disjoint subsets as follow:

$$ \mathcal{A}:=\Big((B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega)\setminus B_{r-2\varepsilon^{9/10}}(x)\Big)\cup\Big((B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega)\cap U_{2\varepsilon^{9/10}}(\partial\Omega)\Big), $$

$$ \mathcal{B}:=\left\{y\in(B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega)\setminus\mathcal{A}\;:\;B_{\varepsilon^{9/10}}(y)\cap\left\{|u|\leq 1-b\right\}\neq\emptyset\right\}, $$

$$ \mathcal{C}:=\left\{y\in(B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega)\setminus\mathcal{A}\;:\;B_{\varepsilon^{9/10}}(y)\cap\left\{|u|\leq 1-b\right\}=\emptyset\right\}. $$

Note that $r\geq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}\geq 2\varepsilon^{9/10}$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ (depending on $c_{6}$ ). We will estimate the (L.H.S.) of (4.28) over each of the three subsets defined above.

We begin with the estimate on $\mathcal{A}$ . By (2.5) and the bound on ball curvatures, for $r_{2}$ small enough (depending only on $n$ , $k_{0}$ and $\kappa_{0}$ ) we have the following volume estimate

$$ dv_{g}(\mathcal{A})\leq C(n)r^{n-1}\varepsilon^{9/10}. $$

Combining this estimate with (4.15) and $r\geq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ , we have

$$ \frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{\mathcal{A}}\xi_{\varepsilon}^{+}(u)\leq C(n)\varepsilon^{1/10}r^{-1}\leq C(n)c_{6}^{-1/8}r^{-7/8} $$

which is clearly bounded by the (R.H.S.) of (4.28) provided that $c_{7}\geq C(n)c_{6}^{-1/8}$ .

We now proceed with the estimate on $\mathcal{B}$ . We first need to an estimate of the volume $dv_{g}(\mathcal{B})$ by considering the covering of $\mathcal{B}$ by balls $\{B_{\varepsilon^{9/10}}(z)\}$ with centers $z\in\left\{|u|\leq 1-b\right\}\cap(\Omega\cap B_{r-\varepsilon^{9/10}}(x)\setminus\overline{U_{\varepsilon^{9/10}}(\partial\Omega)})$ . By Vitali covering lemma, we can extract a finite disjoint family of such balls $\{B_{\varepsilon^{9/10}}(z_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ so that $\mathcal{B}\subset\cup_{i=1}^{N}B_{5\varepsilon^{9/10}}(z_{i})$ . Hence, we have from (2.4) that the volume estimate

$$ dv_{g}(\mathcal{B})\leq N\cdot C(n)\varepsilon^{9n/10} $$

holds for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ depending on $r_{0}$ . It remains to bound $N$ from above. Applying Lemma 4.12 (with $x=z_{i}$ ), since $\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon^{9/10}\leq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ and $\operatorname{dist}(z_{i},\partial\Omega)>\varepsilon^{9/10}$ , we have $I_{\varepsilon,u}(\varepsilon^{9/10},z_{i})\geq c_{6}$ . Summing over all $i$ , noting that $\{B_{\varepsilon^{9/10}}(z_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ are disjoint balls contained in $B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega$ , we have

$$ N\omega_{n-1}c_{6}\varepsilon^{9(n-1)/10}\leq\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}e_{\varepsilon}(u)=\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x). $$

This gives an upper estimate on $N$ . Putting it back to (4.29), we obtain the volume estimate

$$ dv_{g}(\mathcal{B})\leq C(n,c_{6})\varepsilon^{9/10}r^{n-1}I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x). $$

Using this estimate together with (4.15) and $r\geq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ , we have

$$ \frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{\mathcal{B}}\xi_{\varepsilon}^{+}(u)\leq C(n,c_{6})\varepsilon^{1/10}r^{-1}I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq C(n,c_{6})r^{-7/8}I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x) $$

which is clearly bounded by the (R.H.S.) of (4.28) with $c_{7}$ sufficiently large depending only on $n$ and $c_{6}$ .

Finally, it remains to prove the estimate on $\mathcal{C}$ . Consider the Lipschitz function

$$ \phi(y):=\min\left\{1,\varepsilon^{-9/10}\operatorname{dist}_{g}\left(y,(\tilde{U}\setminus(B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega))\cup\left\{|u|\leq 1-b\right\}\right)\right\} $$

which clearly satisfies

- • $\phi=0$ on $(\tilde{U}\setminus(B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega))\cup\left\{|u|\leq 1-b\right\}$ ,

- • $\phi=1$ on $\mathcal{C}$ ,

- • $0\leq\phi\leq 1$ and $|\nabla\phi|\leq\varepsilon^{-9/10}$ everywhere.

Taking gradient on both sides of (4.1) and then multiplying by $\phi^{2}\nabla u$ , we have by Bochner formula (2.3) that

$$ \varepsilon\phi^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\Delta|\nabla u|^{2}-|\operatorname{Hess}u|^{2}+(n-1)k_{0}|\nabla u|^{2}\right)\geq\varepsilon\phi^{2}\langle\nabla\Delta u,\nabla u\rangle=\frac{W^{\prime\prime}(u)}{\varepsilon}\phi^{2}|\nabla u|^{2}. $$

Integrating the above on $B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega$ and integrating by part (note that $\phi=0$ on $B_{r}(x)\cap\partial\Omega$ ), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\left(\varepsilon\phi^{2}|\operatorname{Hess}u|^{2}+\frac{W^{\prime\prime}(u)}{\varepsilon}\phi^{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\right) \displaystyle\leq-\varepsilon\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi\langle\nabla\phi,\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\rangle+C(n,k_{0})\varepsilon\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi^{2}|\nabla u|^{2} \displaystyle=-2\varepsilon\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi\operatorname{Hess}u(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)+C(n,k_{0})\varepsilon\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi^{2}|\nabla u|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\varepsilon\phi^{2}|\operatorname{Hess}u|^{2}+2\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\varepsilon|\nabla u|^{2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}+C(n,k_{0})\varepsilon\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi^{2}|\nabla u|^{2} $$

where we have used Cauchy-Schwarz and Young’s inequalities in the last inequality. Since $\operatorname{spt}\phi\subset\left\{|u|>1-b\right\}$ , we have $W^{\prime\prime}(u)\geq\kappa$ on $\operatorname{spt}\phi$ . Absorbing the first term on right to the left hand side and combining this with $|\nabla\phi|\leq\varepsilon^{-9/10}$ , we obtain for $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small (depending on $n$ , $k_{0}$ and $\kappa$ )

$$ \frac{\kappa}{2\varepsilon}\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi^{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\leq 2\varepsilon^{-4/5}\int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}. $$

Since $\phi=1$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and $0\leq\phi\leq 1$ , together with $r\geq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ , we have

$$ \frac{1}{r^{n}}\int_{\mathcal{C}}\xi_{\varepsilon}^{+}(u)\leq\frac{4\omega_{n-1}}{\kappa}\varepsilon^{1/5}r^{-1}I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq C(n,W,c_{6})r^{-3/4}I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x) $$

which is clearly bounded by the (R.H.S.) of (4.28) with $c_{7}$ sufficiently large depending only on $n$ , $W$ and $c_{6}$ (note that $r^{-3/4}\leq r^{-7/8}$ ). ∎

Using Proposition 4.13, we can extend Lemma 4.12 beyond the scale of $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{4/5})$ .

#### Proposition 4.14 (Energy density ratio lower bound II).

For any $b\in(0,1-\alpha)$ , there exist constants

$$ r_{3}=r_{3}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))\in(0,1), $$

$$ \varepsilon_{8}=\varepsilon_{8}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{8}=c_{8}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0 $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{8}$ , $x\in\partial\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ with $|u(x)|\leq 1-b$ , and $\varepsilon\leq r\leq r_{3}$ , we have

$$ I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\geq c_{8}. $$

In fact, the same holds for $x\in\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ provided furthermore that $r<\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega)$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 4.12, the proposition holds for $\varepsilon\leq r\leq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ with $c_{8}=c_{6}$ and $\varepsilon_{8}=\varepsilon_{6}$ . The point is to use the almost monotonicity formula in Lemma 4.2 and 4.4 together with Proposition 4.13 to show that $I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)$ cannot further decrease too much as $r$ increases beyond the scale $c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ to some definite radius $r_{3}$ to be determined.

We first deal with the case $x\in\partial\Omega$ . By the boundary almost monotonicity formula Lemma 4.4 together with (4.28), for $\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{7}$ we obtain for $c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}\leq\rho\leq\frac{1}{2}\min\{r_{2},i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\tilde{U})\}$ ,

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\omega_{n-1}e^{c_{1}\rho}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\rho,x)\right)\geq-\frac{c_{7}}{\rho^{7/8}}e^{c_{1}\rho}(\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\rho,x)+1). $$

We define $r_{3}$ as the supremum of all $r^{\prime}\in\left[c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},\frac{1}{2}\min\{r_{2},i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\tilde{U})\}\right]$ such that

$$ e^{c_{1}\rho}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\rho,x)\geq\frac{1}{2}c_{6}e^{c_{1}c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}}\text{ for all $\rho\in[c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},r^{\prime}]$}. $$

Note that the left hand side is a continuous function of $\rho$ . By Lemma 4.12, we have $r_{3}>c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ . If $r_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\min\{r_{2},i_{0},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\tilde{U})\}$ , then we are done by taking $\varepsilon_{8}=\min\{\varepsilon_{6},\varepsilon_{7}\}$ and $c_{8}=\frac{1}{4}c_{6}e^{-c_{1}r_{2}}$ (we further reduce $r_{3}$ depending on $k_{0}$ , $\kappa_{0}$ , $C_{0}$ and $\Lambda_{0}$ according to the estimate (4.27)). Otherwise, by continuity we must have

$$ e^{c_{1}r_{3}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r_{3},x)=\frac{1}{2}c_{6}e^{c_{1}c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}}. $$

By the definition of $r_{3}$ and (4.30), we have for $\rho\in[c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},r_{3}]$

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\log\left(e^{c_{1}\rho}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\rho,x)\right)\geq-C(n,c_{6},c_{7},r_{2})\rho^{-7/8}. $$

Integrating $\rho$ over $[c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},r_{3}]$ , using (4.31) and Lemma 4.12,

$$ \log\frac{1}{2}\geq\log\left(\frac{e^{c_{1}r_{3}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r_{3},x)}{e^{c_{1}c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},x)}\right)\geq-8C(n,c_{6},c_{7},r_{2})r_{3}^{1/8}. $$

This gives the desired positive lower bound for $r_{3}$ independent of $\varepsilon$ and $x$ . The proof for the interior case $x\in\Omega$ is similar where we use Lemma 4.2 instead. ∎

We now proceed to establish an upper bound for the energy density ratio in terms of the uniform energy bound $E_{0}$ , within the same range of radii as in Proposition 4.14. Note that we do not require the center point $x$ to lie inside the transition region $\{|u|\leq 1-b\}$ .

#### Proposition 4.15 (Energy density ratio upper bound).

For any $b\in(0,1-\alpha)$ , there exist constants

$$ \varepsilon_{9}=\varepsilon_{9}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{9}=c_{9}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>1 $$

such that for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{9}$ , $x\in\partial\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ , and $\varepsilon\leq r\leq r_{3}$ , we have

$$ I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq c_{9}(E_{0}+1). $$

In fact, the same holds for $x\in\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ provided furthermore that $r<\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega)$ .

#### Proof.

We only give the proof for $x\in\partial\Omega$ as the interior case is similar. We first treat the case when $c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}\leq r\leq r_{3}$ . Let $\delta_{0}:=\max\{1,e^{c_{1}r_{3}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r_{3},x)\}>0$ . Note that

$$ \delta_{0}\leq C(c_{1},n)r_{3}^{-(n-1)}E_{0}+C(c_{1},n)\Lambda_{0}C_{0}\leq C(c_{1},n,r_{3},\Lambda_{0},C_{0})(E_{0}+1). $$

Note that $e^{c_{1}r}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq\delta_{0}$ clearly implies the desired upper bound of $I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)$ . We can assume without loss of generality that $e^{c_{1}\rho}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\rho,x)\geq\delta_{0}$ for all $\rho\in[r,r_{3}]$ . Integrating (4.30) over $[r,r_{3}]$ , we obtain as in Proposition 4.14 that

$$ \log\left(\frac{e^{c_{1}r_{3}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r_{3},x)}{e^{c_{1}r}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)}\right)\geq-C(c_{7},n,c_{1},r_{3}). $$

This implies

$$ \widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq C(c_{7},n,c_{1},r_{3})\delta_{0} $$

which is the desired upper bound by (4.32).

It remains to treat the case $\varepsilon\leq r\leq c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}$ . Integrating the almost monotonicity formula (4.11) over $[r,c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}]$ and using the pointwise bound (4.15), we obtain

$$ e^{c_{1}r}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\leq C(n,c_{1},r_{3},c_{6})+e^{c_{1}c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},x) $$

which yields the desire result as $\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},x)\leq c_{9}(E_{0}+1)$ . ∎

We conclude this section with the following proposition which says that the energy density ratio is almost monotone modulo a term of order $r^{1/8}$ for the range of radii in $[c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},r_{3}]$ .

#### Proposition 4.16 (Almost monotonicity of energy density ratio).

For any $b\in(0,1-\alpha)$ , there exist constants

$$ \varepsilon_{10}=\varepsilon_{10}(b,\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ c_{10}=c_{10}(b,E_{0},\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>1 $$

such that for any $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{10}$ , $x\in\partial\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ and $c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5}\leq s\leq r\leq r_{3}$ , we have

$$ I_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\geq e^{-c_{10}(r-s)}I_{\varepsilon,u}(s,x)-c_{10}r^{1/8}; $$

In fact, the same holds for $x\in\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ provided furthermore that $r<\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ .

#### Proof.

We again just provide the proof for the case $x\in\partial\Omega$ . Using Proposition 4.15 and (4.30), for $\varepsilon<\min\{\varepsilon_{7},\varepsilon_{9}\}$ , we have for $\rho\in[c_{6}\varepsilon^{4/5},r_{3}]$ that

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(e^{c_{1}\rho}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(\rho,x)\right)\geq-C(c_{1},c_{7},c_{9},E_{0})\rho^{-7/8}. $$

Integrating $\rho$ over $[s,r]$ gives

$$ \widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(r,x)\geq e^{-c_{1}(r-s)}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon,u}(s,x)-C(c_{1},c_{7},c_{9},E_{0})r^{1/8}, $$

from which (4.33) easily follows by (4.27) (since $r\leq r^{1/8}$ ). ∎

## 5. Density ratio bounds and rectifiability of the limit varifold

In this section, we assume $u_{i}$ , $\varepsilon_{i}$ and $\lambda_{i}$ are sequences given in Section 3.1. Recall that the associated Radon measures $\mu_{i}$ on $U$ and the associated varifolds $V_{i}\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ are defined in (3.4) and (3.5) respectively. By the compactness of Radon measures, after possibly passing to a subsequence, there exists a Radon measure $\mu$ on $U$ and a varifold $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ such that

$$ \mu_{i}\to\mu\qquad\text{ and }\qquad V_{i}\to V $$

in the sense of measures. Note that $\|V_{i}\|=\mu_{i}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\{|\nabla u_{i}|\neq 0\}}$ from the definition and observe that the support (as measures on $U$ ) of both $\mu$ and $\|V\|$ is contained in $\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ . The main result of this section is to show that $V$ is rectifiable in $U$ and that $\|V\|=\mu$ . Note that the rectifiability of $V$ in the interior of $\Omega$ was established in [21, 17]. Our main point here is to prove that the same continues to hold up to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ .

### 5.1. Density ratio bound

We first begin with a lemma which says that any point in $\operatorname{spt}\mu$ can be approximated by a sequence of points $x_{i}$ in the transition region $\{|u|\leq\alpha\}$ .

#### Lemma 5.1.

For each $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ , there exists (after possibly passing to a subsequence) a sequence $x_{i}\in(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq\alpha\}$ such that $x_{i}\to x$ .

#### Proof.

We argue by contradiction as in the proof of Proposition 4.1 in [21]. Let $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ . We first assume $x\in\partial\Omega$ . Suppose, on the contrary, that there exists some $\overline{r}>0$ such that $B_{\overline{r}}(x)\Subset U$ and $|u_{i}|>\alpha$ on $B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\overline{\Omega}$ for all large $i$ . By shrinking $\overline{r}$ such that $B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\overline{\Omega}$ is connected and passing to a subsequence, we can suppose $u_{i}>\alpha$ . By Lemma 4.8 (shrinking $\overline{r}$ further if necessary) with a fixed $\eta\in(\frac{1}{2},1)$ , we have for all large $i$ that $|u_{i}-1|\leq c_{4}\varepsilon_{i}^{\eta}$ and hence $\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}W(u_{i})=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon_{i}^{2\eta-1})$ on $B_{\overline{r}/3}(x)\cap\Omega$ . We have from Bochner formula (2.3) that for all large $i$ (such that $(n-1)k_{0}\leq\frac{\kappa}{2\varepsilon_{i}}$ )

$$ \Delta\left(\frac{\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}\right)\geq\frac{\kappa}{2\varepsilon_{i}}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}. $$

Multiplying the above by any nonnegative $\phi\in C^{2}_{c}(B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\overline{\Omega})$ and integrating by part, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\Omega}\phi\frac{\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon_{i}^{2}}{\kappa}\int_{B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\Omega}(\Delta\phi)\frac{\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon_{i}^{2}}{\kappa}\int_{B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\partial\Omega}\left(\varepsilon_{i}\phi B(\nabla u_{i},\nabla u_{i})-\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\nu}\frac{\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}\right)d\mathcal{H}^{n-1} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{E_{0}}{\kappa}\varepsilon_{i}^{2}\|\phi\|_{C^{2}}+\frac{1+2\kappa_{0}}{\kappa}\varepsilon_{i}^{2}\|\phi\|_{C^{1}}\int_{B_{\overline{r}}(x)\cap\partial\Omega}e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{i})\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1} $$

where $B$ is the second fundamental form of $\partial\Omega$ . By the proof of Lemma 3.2 together with the estimates $\varepsilon_{i}^{-1}W(u_{i})=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2\eta-1})$ with $\eta>1/2$ and letting $i\to\infty$ , we have $\mu(B_{\overline{r}/3}(x))=0$ , contradicting that $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ . The case $x\notin\partial\Omega$ is indeed simpler. We further shrink $\overline{r}$ such that $B_{2\overline{r}}(x)\Subset\Omega\cap U$ and there are no boundary terms when we integrate by part. ∎

As a key step towards proving the rectifiability of the limit varifold $V$ , we now establish an up-to-the-boundary locally uniform density ratio upper bound for the limit measure $\mu$ . Note that compared to [21, Proposition 4.1]), we do not claim at this stage that there is a uniform lower bound for the density ratio centered at a boundary point. This is due to the possible complication that the $x_{i}$ ’s in Lemma 5.1 could be a sequence of interior points approaching a boundary point $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu\cap\partial\Omega$ . This poses new difficulties when we want to apply monotonicity formulas which are either centered at a boundary point (Lemma 4.4) or stays away from the boundary (Lemma 4.2).

#### Proposition 5.2 (Density ratio bounds for the limit measure).

There exist constants

$$ \theta_{1}=\theta_{1}(\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0, $$

$$ \theta_{2}=\theta_{2}(E_{0},\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U))>0 $$

such that for any $x\in(\operatorname{spt}\mu\cap\tilde{U})\cap\partial\Omega$ , we have for all $0<r<\frac{r_{3}}{2}$ ,

$$ \frac{\mu(B_{r}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\leq\theta_{2}. $$

Moreover, for any $x\in(\operatorname{spt}\mu\cap\tilde{U})\cap\Omega$ , we have for all $0<r<\frac{1}{2}\min\{r_{3},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega)\}$ ,

$$ \theta_{1}\leq\frac{\mu(B_{r}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\leq\theta_{2}. $$

Here, $r_{3}$ is the constant appearing in Proposition 4.14 with $b=\frac{1-\alpha}{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $x\in(\operatorname{spt}\mu\cap\tilde{U})\cap\partial\Omega$ . Fix any $0<r<\frac{r_{3}}{2}$ . Since $\mu_{i}\to\mu$ as measures, we will have for all large $i$

$$ \frac{\mu(B_{r}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\leq\frac{2\mu_{i}(B_{r}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}=\frac{2}{h_{0}}I_{\varepsilon_{i},u_{i}}(r,x). $$

Hence, the desired assertion follows from Proposition 4.15 with $\theta_{2}:=\frac{2}{h_{0}}c_{9}(E_{0}+1)$ .

For $x\in(\operatorname{spt}\mu\cap\tilde{U})\cap\Omega$ . By Lemma 5.1, after passing to a subsequence, we have a sequence of interior points $x_{i}\in\Omega\cap\tilde{U}$ such that $|u_{i}(x_{i})|\leq\alpha$ for all $i$ and $x_{i}\to x$ . Fix any $0<r<\frac{1}{2}\min\{r_{3},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(x,\partial\Omega)\}$ . The upper bound $\theta_{2}$ is obtained exactly as before. For the lower bound, we observe for all large $i$

$$ \frac{\mu(B_{r}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\geq\frac{\mu_{i}(B_{r}(x))}{2\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\geq\frac{\mu_{i}(B_{r/2}(x_{i}))}{2\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}=\frac{1}{2^{n}h_{0}}I_{\varepsilon_{i},u_{i}}(r/2,x_{i}). $$

Hence, the desired assertion follows from Proposition 4.14 with $\theta_{1}:=\frac{c_{8}}{2^{n}h_{0}}$ . ∎

Exactly the same arguments as in the proof of Lemma 5.1 and Proposition 5.2 yields the following result.

#### Proposition 5.3 (Uniform convergence away from limit interface).

Either $u_{i}\to 1$ or $u_{i}\to-1$ locally uniformly on $(\Omega\cap U)\setminus\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . In particular, we have $M:=\partial^{*}\{u=1\}\subset\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap(\Omega\cap U)$ . Moreover, $\frac{\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}$ and $\frac{W(u_{i})}{\varepsilon_{i}}$ both converges locally uniformly to $0$ on $(\Omega\cap U)\setminus\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ .

### 5.2. Vanishing of discrepancy measure

Let $e_{i}:=e_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{i})$ and $\xi_{i}:=\xi_{\varepsilon_{i}}(u_{i})$ denote the energy density and discrepancy function as defined in (4.3) and (4.4). By compactness of Radon measures (on $U$ ), after possibly passing to a subsequence, we can assume that there exists a Radon measure $|\xi|$ on $U$ such that

$$ |\xi_{i}|dv_{g}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\Omega\cap U}\to|\xi| $$

in the sense of measures. We call $|\xi|$ the discrepancy measure. Since $|\xi_{i}|\leq e_{i}$ , we clearly have $\operatorname{spt}|\xi|\subset\operatorname{spt}\mu\subset\overline{\Omega}\cap U$ .

#### Theorem 5.4 (Vanishing of discrepancy measure).

The discrepancy measure $|\xi|$ vanishes on $U$ , i.e. $|\xi|=0$ . In other words, the discrepancy function $\xi_{i}$ converges to $0$ in $L^{1}_{loc}(\overline{\Omega}\cap U)$ .

#### Proof.

We first claim that for all $x\in\operatorname{spt}|\xi|\cap\partial\Omega$ , we have

$$ \liminf_{r\to 0}\frac{|\xi|(B_{r}(x))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}=0. $$

We argue by contradiction as in [21, Proposition 4.3]. Suppose on the contrary that (5.5) does not hold, i.e. there exist $\delta_{0}>0$ , $R_{0}>0$ and $x_{0}\in\operatorname{spt}|\xi|\cap\partial\Omega$ such that

$$ |\xi|(B_{r}(x_{0}))\geq\delta_{0}\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}\quad\text{ for all $0<r\leq R_{0}$.} $$

By the density ratio upper bound (5.2), there exists $\theta_{2}>0$ such that

$$ \frac{\mu(B_{r}(x_{0}))}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\leq\theta_{2}\quad\text{ for all $0<r\leq\frac{r_{3}}{2}$.} $$

Fix $0<t<\min\{R_{0},\frac{r_{3}}{2},r_{1},r_{2},\frac{1}{\kappa_{0}}\}$ which will be chosen later. Since $|\xi_{i}|dv_{g}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\Omega\cap U}\to|\xi|$ and $\mu_{i}\to\mu$ , by (5.6) and (5.7), for any fixed $N\in\mathbb{N}$ , there exists some $i>N$ such that

$$ \frac{1}{\omega_{n-1}r^{n-1}}\int_{B_{r}(x_{0})\cap\Omega}|\xi_{i}|\geq\frac{\delta_{0}}{2}\quad\text{ for all $r\in[t^{2},t]$} $$

and

$$ \frac{\mu_{i}(B_{t}(x_{0}))}{\omega_{n-1}t^{n-1}}\leq 2\theta_{2}. $$

Note that $|\xi_{i}|=\xi_{i}^{+}+\xi_{i}^{-}$ . By (5.8) and Proposition 4.13, for all $i$ large enough (so that $\varepsilon_{i}<\varepsilon_{7}$ and $c_{6}\varepsilon_{i}^{4/5}\leq t^{2}$ ) we have for all $\rho\in[t^{2},t]$

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{(1+3\kappa_{0}\rho)\rho^{n}}\int_{B_{\rho}(x_{0})\cap\Omega}-\xi_{i} \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{4\rho^{n}}\int_{B_{\rho}(x_{0})\cap\Omega}|\xi_{i}|-\frac{2}{\rho^{n}}\int_{B_{\rho}(x_{0})\cap\Omega}\xi_{i}^{+} \displaystyle\geq\frac{\delta_{0}}{8}\rho^{-1}-\frac{2c_{7}}{\rho^{7/8}}(I_{\varepsilon_{i},u_{i}}(\rho,x_{0})+1). $$

Since $x_{0}\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ , by Proposition 4.15, for all $i$ large enough (so that $\varepsilon_{i}<\min\{\varepsilon_{9},t^{2}\}$ ), we have for all $\rho\in[t^{2},t]$

$$ \frac{1}{(1+3\kappa_{0}\rho)\rho^{n}}\int_{B_{\rho}(x_{0})\cap\Omega}-\xi_{i}\geq\frac{\delta_{0}}{8}\rho^{-1}-C(c_{7},c_{9},E_{0})\rho^{-7/8}. $$

By the almost monotonicity formula (4.11) (note that $\widetilde{\xi}_{i}\leq\xi_{i}$ ), we have for all $\rho\in[t^{2},t]$

$$ \frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\omega_{n-1}e^{c_{1}\rho}\widetilde{I}_{\varepsilon_{i},u_{i}}(\rho,x_{0})\right)\geq\frac{\delta_{0}}{8}e^{c_{1}\rho}\rho^{-1}-C(c_{7},c_{9},E_{0})e^{c_{1}\rho}\rho^{-7/8} $$

Integrating over $[t^{2},t]$ and using (4.27), (5.9), we obtain

$$ C(n,c_{1},\Lambda_{0},C_{0})\left(\frac{h_{0}}{\omega_{n-1}}2\theta_{2}+t\right)\geq\frac{\delta_{0}}{8}\log\frac{1}{t}-C(c_{7},c_{9},E_{0},c_{1})t^{1/8}, $$

which gives a contradiction if $t$ is chosen sufficiently small. Hence, we have proved (5.5).

By the theory of differentiation for Radon measures (applied to $|\xi|$ and $d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\partial\Omega}$ ), c.f. [36, P.26], we conclude from (5.5) that $|\xi|(\partial\Omega)=0$ , i.e. $|\xi|$ vanishes on $\partial\Omega$ . By a similar argument using the interior monotonicity formula (4.9), we can show that (5.5) also holds for interior points $x\in\operatorname{spt}|\xi|\cap\Omega$ . Combining this with the density lower bound in (5.3), we have

$$ \liminf_{r\to 0}\frac{|\xi|(B_{r}(x))}{\mu(B_{r}(x))}=0, $$

from which again implies $|\xi|=0$ inside $\Omega\cap U$ as well. ∎

### 5.3. Rectifiability of limit varifold

Let $V_{i}$ be the varifold associated with $u_{i}$ as in (3.5). After passing to a subsequence, we can also assume that there exist $u\in BV(\Omega\cap U)$ , $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ such that

$$ \lambda_{i}\to\lambda,\quad u_{i}\to u\;a.e.,\quad V_{i}\to V\;\textrm{in the varifold sense.} $$

Our goal is to show that $V$ is in fact rectifiable up to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ . Using the vanishing of the discrepancy measure $|\xi|$ , we can establish the following result. Recall that $M:=\partial^{*}\{u=1\}$ is the reduced boundary of $\{u=1\}$ in $\Omega\cap U$ with outward normal $\nu_{M}$ .

#### Lemma 5.5 (First variation of limit varifold).

There exist a constant

$$ c_{11}=c_{11}(E_{0},\Lambda_{0},C_{0},W,n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},\operatorname{dist}_{g}(\tilde{U},\partial U),dv_{g}(\Omega\cap U),\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(\partial\Omega\cap U))>1 $$

such that for any $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ with $\operatorname{spt}X\subset\tilde{U}$ , we have

$$ \left|h_{0}\delta V(X)+\lambda\int_{\Omega\cap U}X\cdot Du\right|\leq c_{11}\sup_{\partial\Omega\cap U}|X\cdot\nu|. $$

In particular, for any $X\in\mathfrak{X}^{tan}_{c}(U)$ , we have

$$ \delta V(X)=-\frac{2\lambda}{h_{0}}\int_{M}X\cdot\nu_{M}\;d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

#### Remark 5.6.

If $\lambda=0$ , then (5.13) implies that $V$ is a free boundary stationary varifold (c.f. [16, Definition 3.1]).

#### Proof.

Let $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}(U)$ with $\operatorname{spt}X\subset\tilde{U}$ . Note that $\delta V_{i}(X)\to\delta V(X)$ as $i\to\infty$ . On the other hand, by the calculations in [23, Lemma 4.1], we have

$$ \displaystyle h_{0}\delta V_{i}(X)= \displaystyle\int_{\Omega\cap\{|\nabla u_{i}|\neq 0\}}\nabla X\cdot\left(\frac{\nabla u_{i}}{|\nabla u_{i}|}\otimes\frac{\nabla u_{i}}{|\nabla u_{i}|}\right)\xi_{i}-\int_{\Omega\cap\{|\nabla u_{i}|=0\}}(\nabla X\cdot I)\frac{W(u_{i})}{\varepsilon_{i}} \displaystyle+\lambda_{i}\int_{\Omega}u_{i}\operatorname{div}_{g}X+\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{W(u_{i})}{\varepsilon_{i}}-\lambda_{i}u_{i}\right)(X\cdot\nu)d\mathcal{H}^{n-1}. $$

Note that the first and second term of the (R.H.S.) above are both bounded by $C(n)\|X\|_{C^{1}}\int_{\tilde{U}\cap\Omega}|\xi_{i}|$ , which converges to $0$ as $i\to\infty$ by Theorem 5.4. For the third term, since $\lambda_{i}\to\lambda$ and $u_{i}\to u\in BV(\Omega\cap U)$ a.e., by Dominated Convergence theorem we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\lambda_{i}\int_{\Omega}u_{i}\operatorname{div}_{g}X=\lambda\int_{\Omega}u\operatorname{div}_{g}X=-\lambda\int_{\Omega}X\cdot Du+\lambda\int_{\partial\Omega}Tu(X\cdot\nu)d\mathcal{H}^{n-1} $$

where $Tu\in L^{1}(\partial\Omega)$ is the trace of $u$ on $\partial\Omega$ (c.f. [13, Theorem 5.6]). Moreover, by the boundednesss of the trace operator $T$ , we have

$$ \|Tu\|_{L^{1}(\partial\Omega\cap U)}\leq C(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0})\|u\|_{BV(\Omega\cap U)}\leq C(n,i_{0},k_{0},\kappa_{0},E_{0},W,dv_{g}(\Omega\cap U)). $$

Combining all the above and applying Lemma 3.2 for the last term gives (5.12). ∎

#### Theorem 5.7 (Rectifiability of limit varifold).

The limit varifold $V\in\mathbf{V}_{n-1}(U)$ satisfies $\|V\|=\mu$ and is rectifiable.

#### Proof.

Recall that $\|V_{i}\|=\mu_{i}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\{|\nabla u_{i}|\neq 0\}}$ and since $h_{0}\mu_{i}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\{|\nabla u_{i}|=0\}}\leq|\xi_{i}|dv_{g}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}{\Omega\cap U}$ which converges to $0$ by Theorem 5.4, we have $\|V_{i}\|\to\mu$ and thus $\|V\|=\mu$ . From (5.12), we know that $V$ has locally bounded first variation in $U$ . By Allard’s Rectifiability Theorem [36, Theorem 42.4], it remains to show that $\|V\|=\mu$ has a locally uniform density lower bound on $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ .

We claim that $V$ has free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ as described in Section 2.4. Recall $M=\partial^{*}\{u=1\}\subset\Omega\cap U$ . By the structure theorem for sets of finite perimeter (c.f. [13, Theorem 5.15], $\|\partial\{u=1\}\|=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}M$ which is a Radon measure on $U$ by (3.3). Consider the Radon measures $\mu=\|V\|$ and $\sigma:=\mathcal{H}^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}M$ on $U$ , the density ratio lower bound (5.3) implies (c.f. [13, Section 1.6]) that $\sigma$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$ . Together with Lemma 5.5, the Radon-Nikodym Theorem implies that

$$ \delta V(X)=-\frac{2\lambda}{h_{0}}\int_{\Omega\cap U}X\cdot\nu_{M}d\sigma=-\frac{2\lambda}{h_{0}}\int_{\Omega\cap U}(X\cdot\nu_{M})D_{\mu}\sigma d\mu $$

for any $X\in\mathfrak{X}_{c}^{tan}(U)$ . Therefore, $V$ has free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ with $\|V\|$ -measurable vector field

$$ H^{T}(x):=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\frac{2\lambda}{h_{0}}(D_{\mu}\sigma)\nu_{M}&\text{ for $x\in M$,}\\
0&\text{ otherwise.}\end{array}\right. $$

Note the the density lower bound in Proposition 5.2 implies that $H^{T}\in L^{\infty}$ .

To finish the proof, note that $\|V\|$ has a locally uniform density lower bound on $\operatorname{spt}\|V\|\cap\Omega\cap U$ by (5.3). As $V$ has free boundary in $\partial\Omega\cap U$ with $H^{T}\in L^{\infty}$ , the “reflected” density of $V$ is upper semi-continuous (c.f. [15, Corollary 3.2]) and hence $\|V\|$ has a locally uniform density lower bound up to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ . This completes the proof. ∎

We now give the proof of our main result, Theorem 3.3, modulo the integrality of the limit varifold $V$ which will be presented in the next section.

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3.

(1) follows directly from Theorem 5.4 and 5.7. (2) follows from Lemma 5.1, Proposition 5.2 and 5.3. The proof of (3) will be given in Section 6.Finally, (4) follows from the proof of Theorem 5.7 and that $\Theta(x)=(D_{\mu}\sigma(x))^{-1}$ . The rest then follows from [12, Proposition 3.2]. ∎

## 6. Integrality of the limit varifold

We will establish in this section that the limit varifold $V$ is integral in $U$ , i.e. $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ . Since $V$ is rectifiable in $U$ by Theorem 5.7, $V$ has a unique approximate tangent space $T$ at $\mathcal{H}^{n-1}$ -a.e. $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ . In other words, for any such $x\in\operatorname{spt}\|V\|$ and any sequence of positive real numbers $r_{i}\to 0$ , we have

$$ (\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V\to\Theta(x)|T| $$

as varifolds 33 3 To be more precise, one can first locally isometrically embed $(\tilde{M},g)$ into some Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{L}$ and then do rescalings in $\mathbb{R}^{L}$ (c.f. [2]). Alternatively, one can also do the rescalings intrinsically using the exponential map (c.f. [35]). Both are equivalent and thus we will be using either formulation. Here, $(\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V$ is the pushforward of the varifold $V$ by the map $\Phi_{r_{i}}:(\widetilde{M},g)\to(\widetilde{M},r_{i}^{-2}g)$ , $\Theta(x)$ is the $(n-1)$ -dimensional density of $V$ at $x$ and $|T|$ is the unit density varifold associated to the hyperplane $T\subset T_{x}\widetilde{M}\cong\mathbb{R}^{n}$ .

We shall assume $x\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ as the arguments for interior points are similar (see also [21, 38, 40] in the Euclidean setting). Fix any $r_{i}\to 0$ . We use $\tilde{g}_{i}:=r_{i}^{-2}g$ to denote the rescaled metric on $\widetilde{M}$ . Note that $(\overline{\Omega}\cap U,x,\tilde{g}_{i})\to(\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+},0,g_{E})$ smoothly in the sense of pointed Cheeger-Gromov convergence. Here $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}:=\{(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;:\;x_{n}\geq 0\}$ is the upper half-space equipped with the standard Euclidean metric $g_{E}$ . Since $V_{i}\to V$ , after passing to a subsequence, we can further assume as $i\to\infty$

$$ (\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}\to\Theta(x)|T|\quad\text{ and }\quad\varepsilon_{i}r_{i}^{-1}\to 0. $$

Let $\tilde{V}_{i}=(\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}=\varepsilon_{i}r_{i}^{-1}$ and $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}=r_{i}\lambda_{i}$ . Then $u_{i}$ satisfies, with respect to the rescaled metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ ,

$$ -\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}\Delta_{\tilde{g}_{i}}u_{i}+\frac{W^{\prime}(u_{i})}{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}=\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\quad\text{in $\Omega\cap U$}, $$

$$ \frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\text{on $\partial\Omega\cap U$}. $$

Note that we have $\|u_{i}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{0}$ , $|\tilde{\lambda}_{i}|\leq r_{i}\Lambda_{0}\to 0$ . Moreover, by Proposition 4.15, for any fixed $R>0$ , we have for all sufficiently large $i$

$$ (E_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}\mathbin{\vrule height=6.88889pt,depth=0.0pt,width=0.55974pt\vrule height=0.55974pt,depth=0.0pt,width=5.59721pt}(B_{R}(x),\tilde{g}_{i}))(u_{i})=\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}I_{\varepsilon_{i},u_{i}}(r_{i}R,x)\leq\omega_{n-1}R^{n-1}c_{9}(E_{0}+1). $$

Therefore, all the results obtained in previous sections can be applied (with slight modifications for a convergent sequence of varying metrics). Observe that $\tilde{V}_{i}$ is the associated varifold of $u_{i}$ with respect to the rescaled metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ and $\tilde{V}_{i}\to\tilde{V}:=\Theta(x)|T|$ . Since $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\to 0$ , by Lemma 5.5, $\tilde{V}_{i}\to\tilde{V}:=\Theta(x)|T|$ is a stationary varifold with free boundary in $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:=\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ . As $\tilde{V}$ is supported in $\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $T$ is a hyperplane, we must have $T=\{x_{n}=0\}$ .

For our convenience, by a suitable choice of coordinates, we can assume $\overline{\Omega}=\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ is equipped with a metric $\tilde{g}_{i}$ converging locally smoothly to the Euclidean metric $g_{E}$ and $U=B_{4}(0)$ is the Euclidean ball of radius $4$ centered at the origin. All the balls and distances will be taken with respect to $g_{E}$ from now on. As in Section 4, we denote throughout this section $u_{i}$ , $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}$ , $\tilde{g}_{i}$ by $u$ , $\tilde{\lambda}$ , $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ , $\tilde{g}$ . We use $T:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ to denote the orthogonal projection $T(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n-1})$ with respect to $g_{E}$ and $T^{\perp}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$ to denote the map $T^{\perp}(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})=x_{n}$ . We also define $\nu=(\nu_{1},\cdots,\nu_{n})$ to be the unit normal to the level sets of $u$ as

$$ \nu:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\frac{\nabla u}{|\nabla u|}&\text{ when $|\nabla u|\neq 0$,}\\
0&\text{ when $|\nabla u|=0$.}\end{array}\right. $$

We also denote

$$ e_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}:=\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}+\frac{W(u)}{\tilde{\varepsilon}},\quad\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}:=\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}}{2}-\frac{W(u)}{\tilde{\varepsilon}}. $$

We first establish a proposition which shows that the smallness of the discrepancy and tilt excess imply the solution $u$ is close in $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ -scale to the one-dimensional heteroclinic solution near the transition region which must be rather far away from the boundary.

#### Proposition 6.1 (Sheets separation).

For any given $s,b\in(0,1)$ , there exist constants

$$ \eta_{1}=\eta_{1}(s,b,W)\in(0,1), $$

$$ L=L(s,b,W)>1 $$

such that the following holds: for any $0<\eta<\eta_{1}$ , suppose we have

- (i) $y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ with $T(y)=0$ and $|u(y)|\leq 1-b$ ;

- (ii) $u$ satisfies (6.2) on $B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and (6.3) along $B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ with $\tilde{\varepsilon}\in(0,1)$ , $|\tilde{\lambda}|\leq\eta$ , $\|\tilde{g}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y))}\leq\eta$ and $|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|\leq\eta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{-1}$ on $B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ ;

- (iii)

$$ \int_{B_{4\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|+(1-(\nu_{n})^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon}|\nabla u|^{2}\leq\eta(4\tilde{\varepsilon}L)^{n-1}, $$

then $B_{3\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}=\emptyset$ , $T^{-1}(0)\cap\{x\in B_{3\tilde{\varepsilon}L}(y):u(x)=u(y)\}=\{y\}$ and

Exactly the same proof (the weaker hypothesis $|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}|\leq\eta\tilde{\varepsilon}^{-1}$ is sufficient as pointed out in [38, Proposition 4.8]) of [21, Proposition 5.6] goes through using the up-to-the-boundary $C^{2}$ -estimates in [1] and shows that $u$ is in $\tilde{\varepsilon}$ -scale $C^{1}$ -close to the unique one-dimensional finite-energy heteroclinic solution $q(x_{n})$ satisfying $q(|y|)=u(y)$ . The second proposition deals with decomposing the limit varifold $V$ into stacked single-layered interfaces. $$ Z_{\alpha}:=\left\{x\in B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\;:\;|u(x)|\leq\frac{1+\alpha}{2}\right\}. $$

#### Lemma 6.4.

$$ \varepsilon_{13}=\varepsilon_{13}(W)>0, $$

$$ \left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}\Delta\psi_{R}=\frac{\kappa}{4}\psi_{R}&\text{on $B_{R}(0)\cap\tilde{\Omega}$},\\

#### Lemma 6.5.

$$ \mathcal{L}^{n}\left(\{x\in B_{3}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\;:\;\operatorname{dist}(x,Z_{\alpha})<r\}\right)\leq c_{14}r. $$

#### Proof.

The proof follows the same covering arguments from [21, Lemma 5.3] using Proposition 4.14 (with $b=\frac{1-\alpha}{2}$ ) and the arguments in the proof of Proposition 4.13. ∎

#### Proof of Proposition 6.3.

It follows exactly the same proof in [21, Proposition 5.1] using Lemma 6.4 and 6.5. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.3 (continued).

We now finish the proof of Theorem 3.3 by showing that $V\in\mathbf{IV}_{n-1}(U)$ . We use the same notations as in the beginning of this section with $x=0\in\partial\Omega\cap U$ . Recall that

$$ \tilde{V}_{i}:=(\Phi_{r_{i}})_{\sharp}V_{i}\to\Theta_{0}|T|\quad\text{ and }\quad\tilde{\varepsilon_{i}}:=\varepsilon_{i}r_{i}^{-1}\to 0. $$

Our goal here is to prove that $\Theta_{0}\in\mathbb{N}$ .

First of all, by Theorem 5.4 and (6.7), we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}|=\lim_{i\to\infty}\int_{B_{4}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}(1-\nu_{n}^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon_{i}}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}=0. $$

Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$ be the smallest positive integer such that $N>\Theta_{0}$ . Note that $\|\tilde{g}_{i}-g_{E}\|_{C^{2}(B_{R}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+})}\to 0$ and $|\tilde{\lambda}_{i}|\to 0$ as $i\to\infty$ . Fix an arbitrary small $s>0$ , by Proposition 6.3 and (6.8), we can choose some $b>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $i$ , we have

$$ \int_{B_{3}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\geq 1-b\}}\left(\frac{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{W(u_{i})}{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}\right)\leq s. $$

With these choices of $s$ and $b$ , we choose $0<\eta<\min\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\}$ and $L>1$ as in Proposition 6.1 and 6.2 (with $R=1$ and $\tilde{E}_{0}=c_{9}(E_{0}+1)$ ). We then define as in [21] the good set $G_{i}$ consisting of all $x\in B_{2}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}$ such that

$$ \int_{B_{r}(x)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}}|\xi_{\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}}|+(1-\nu_{n}^{2})\tilde{\varepsilon_{i}}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}\leq\eta r^{n-1}\quad\textrm{for all $r\in[4\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}L,1]$.} $$

By Besicovitch covering theorem and (6.8), we have

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\|\tilde{V}_{i}\|(B_{2}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}\setminus G_{i})=0 $$

and

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\mathcal{H}^{n-1}(T(B_{2}(0)\cap\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\cap\{|u_{i}|\leq 1-b\}\setminus G_{i}))=0. $$

On the other hand, by (6.7) and Proposition 4.14, we obtain

$$ \lim_{i\to\infty}\operatorname{dist}(G_{i},T)=0. $$

Now, for any $x\in B_{1}(0)\cap\partial\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$ and $|t|\leq 1-b$ , we let

$$ Y:=T^{-1}(x)\cap G_{i}\cap\{u_{i}=t\}\qquad\textrm{ and }\qquad a:=L\tilde{\varepsilon}_{i}. $$

We would like to apply Proposition 6.2 to this $Y$ for all sufficiently large $i$ . Note that $\|\tilde{g}_{i}-g_{E}\|\to 0$ and $\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\to 0$ as $i\to\infty$ . By Proposition 6.1 and (6.10), all assumptions in (i) of Proposition 6.2 are satisfied (except perhaps the cardinality of $Y$ ) for large $i$ . Noting how the constants in Section 4 scale with respect to the blow-up radii $r_{i}\to 0$ (especially Proposition 4.10 and 4.13), (ii) is also satisfied for large $i$ . Condition (iii) is essentially the definition of $G_{i}$ , together with Proposition 4.15. Note that $Y$ cannot contain more than $N-1$ elements since otherwise we will obtain by Proposition 6.1 and 6.2 that

$$ N\leq(N+1)s+(1+s)(\Theta_{0}+s) $$

which is a contradiction when $s$ is sufficiently small (depending only on $N$ ). The rest of the argument is the same as [21, Theorem 1] and we must have $\Theta_{0}=N-1\in\mathbb{N}$ . ∎
